signals.description: Real-time and forecast load-shedding stages. Load shedding ended in mid-May 2025 and SA marked 12 consecutive months without cuts by mid-2026. However, Eskom warnings about emergency reserve depletion and ageing coal retirements (2026–2030 gap) are recurring triggers for C&I solar decisions. An escalation back to even Stage 2 would immediately restart procurement pipelines.

Each NERSA tariff increase compresses industrial electricity margins and directly improves solar ROI/payback calculations. NERSA approved 12.74% for FY2026 and 8.76% for FY2027. Announcements trigger procurement reviews from CFOs and energy managers within 30–60 days.

signals.type: Municipal Energy Notices and SSEG Approval News
signals.description: 35+ municipalities have approved SSEG tariff structures as of 2026. NERSA's national net-billing framework (approved December 2024) standardises prosumer credits. Municipalities granting SSEG connection approvals and Eskom extending its SSEG registration fee waiver to September 2026 both signal active demand. Monitoring NERSA and SAPVIA for new municipal approvals reveals lead-generation geographies.

The enhanced Section 12BA (125%) expired 28 February 2025 — future renewals or new incentives would create procurement surges.

CIDB.relevant_classes: EP (Electrical Engineering Infrastructure) or EB (Electrical Engineering Building); ME (Mechanical Engineering) for hybrid projects with HVAC or pump systems
CIDB.grades_for_large_industrial_tenders: Grade 7EP for tenders up to ~R40M; Grade 8EP for tenders up to ~R130M; Grade 9EP (no upper limit) required for major SOE and multinational mining contracts. Typical large industrial and mining contracts require Grade 7–9EP.

DOL_electrical_contractor.description: Registration with the Department of Labour (DoL) as an electrical contractor is a legal requirement under the Electrical Installation Regulations (2009). Annual renewal fee of R120. Required before any paid electrical installation work.

ECB.description: Electrical Conformance Board (ECB) listing is voluntary since DoL took over contractor registration in 2012, but ECB listing is viewed positively in tender evaluations for industrial and commercial projects. Provides added credibility marker.

registration_requirements.wiremans_licence: A Wireman's Licence (issued by DoL via trade test) is required for the responsible person on all electrical installation work. Essential for electrical contractor operability.
registration_requirements.BBBEE: A valid B-BBEE certificate (or EME sworn affidavit for entities under R10M annual turnover) is mandatory for all government and SOE tender submissions. Level 1–4 preferred for scoring advantage.
registration_requirements.additional_note: ECA SA (Electrical Contractors Association South Africa) issued an April 2026 warning against unqualified solar installations. Membership of ECA SA and adherence to SANS 10142-1 (wiring code) are increasingly referenced in large tender specifications.

market_context.briefing:
South Africa recorded 12 consecutive months without load shedding as of mid-2026, with rolling power cuts last imposed in May 2025. Eskom's generation recovery was driven by reduced unplanned outages and improved maintenance, but retiring coal capacity from 2026 to 2030 creates a structural supply gap. New renewable additions must come online on schedule to prevent a return to outages — a credible risk that keeps energy-security arguments alive in industrial boardrooms.

Despite the end of load shedding, demand for solar and electrical solutions remains strong. The investment driver has shifted from 'security' to 'cost reduction': NERSA-approved Eskom tariff increases of 12.74% (FY2026) and 8.76% (FY2027) continue to compress industrial electricity margins, delivering strong solar ROI for businesses. South Africa added 1.6 GW of new solar in 2025, with total installed capacity at 9.76 GW by 2026 and projected to reach 16.88 GW by 2031.

On regulation, NERSA approved a national net-billing framework (December 2024) that standardises prosumer credits for grid-exported solar. A March 2026 registration deadline for all SSEG systems up to 50 kW was set. DMRE's eased wheeling regulations and Eskom's Virtual Wheeling programme now allow industrial groups with multi-site footprints to contract solar power from remote generators without complex municipal billing adjustments. The NERSA MYPD6 congestion curtailment mechanism (4% cap) has unlocked ~1.5 GW of new capacity in the Western and Eastern Cape for private developers.

On incentives, the enhanced Section 12BA (125% first-year deduction) expired 28 February 2025. The permanent Section 12B remains active: solar PV up to 1 MW qualifies for a 100% first-year deduction; systems above 1 MW use the 50/30/20 schedule. VAT-registered businesses may additionally claim input VAT on installation costs. These incentives compress payback periods for CAPEX buyers, keeping both financed and direct-purchase pipelines active.

typical_system_sizes.commercial_offices_retail_warehouses: 100 kW – 1 MW rooftop or ground-mount; suits light manufacturing, warehouses, retail chains, office parks
typical_system_sizes.industrial_manufacturing_food_and_bevera: 1 MW – 10 MW; multi-phase behind-the-meter rollouts; e.g., NCP Chlorchem 27 MWp (multi-phase)
typical_system_sizes.mining_and_heavy_industry: 10 MW – 340+ MW; dedicated private power plants under CPPA or Eskom Virtual Wheeling; e.g., Glencore 100 MW ferrochrome plant (JUWI), Bolobedu 148 MW (Voltalia for Richards Bay Minerals)
typical_system_sizes.context: Approximately 100 MW of projects between 100 kW and 1 MW and ~250 MW of projects between 1 MW and 50 MW were registered in South Africa in the 12 months to mid-2026, confirming strong C&I mid-market activity.

installed_cost_ranges_per_kW.small_commercial_100kW_to_1MW: R13,000 – R18,000 per kW (fully installed, including inverters, DC cabling, and balance-of-system; no BESS)
installed_cost_ranges_per_kW.medium_industrial_1MW_to_10MW: R10,000 – R14,000 per kW (EPC contract basis; economies of scale reduce BOS and design costs)
installed_cost_ranges_per_kW.large_scale_mining_industrial_10MW_plus: R7,000 – R12,000 per kW (competitive EPC bid pricing at scale; site-specific civil works can push costs higher)

installed_cost_ranges_per_kW.note: Installed costs are highly project-specific. Large civil works (remote sites, grid connection infrastructure) can materially increase per-kW cost.

financing_structures.description: Client purchases and owns the system outright. Qualifies fully for Section 12B tax deductions. Preferred by balance-sheet-strong industrials and mining houses with access to corporate finance or green loan facilities.
financing_structures.typical_providers: Absa, Standard Bank, Nedbank, FNB green/sustainability-linked finance at prime+1% to prime+3% over 5–7 years.

financing_structures.description: Developer finances, owns, and operates the system on the client's site. Client pays a fixed or escalating R/kWh rate below the Eskom tariff — zero upfront capital. Typical contract terms of 10–20 years.
financing_structures.typical_providers: SolarAfrica, GreenYellow SA, GreenHouse Capital, Terra Firma, IMPOWER.

financing_structures.description: Client leases the system with a buy-out option at end of term. Monthly payment replaces most of the Eskom bill. Popular in the SME and light-commercial segment.

A large-scale solar plant is built at a remote site; power is delivered to the industrial/mining client via Eskom's Virtual Wheeling programme. No physical installation at the client's site. Preferred for clients with very high demand (>5 MW).
financing_structures.typical_providers: Voltalia, Pele Green Energy, JUWI, SolarAfrica for utility-scale industrial and mining clients.

common_customer_complaints_with_solar_in: Missed or late installation appointments after the initial quote; poor project scheduling and coordination.
Delayed equipment delivery; components collected from multiple locations rather than delivered as a coordinated project package.
Poor after-sales service: inverter faults go unresolved for weeks; warranty repairs handed off to third parties with no communication or status updates.
Inadequate structural assessments before installation — failure to evaluate roof integrity has led to solar array collapses during adverse weather events.
Use of substandard, uncertified, or grey-market components by installers who have no local technical support channels from their suppliers.
System underperformance of 30–50% below design yield due to incorrect sizing, shading analysis failures, or poor installation workmanship.
Non-compliance with Certificate of Compliance (CoC) and SSEG registration requirements — leaves clients exposed to insurance voidance and grid-connection penalties.
Unqualified or uncertified installers operating without DoL contractor registration or ECB listing — flagged specifically by ECA SA in an April 2026 industry warning.
Poor or no knowledge transfer to client operations team — clients unable to monitor or manage systems post-installation.
